column2: The unexpected visitor had been sent by Zhou Lichun of Jiading. Zhou was in touch with Liu Lichuan and intended to rise in Jiading as soon as the uprising began in Shanghai. He had approached You Laowu beforehand, proposing that they “share good fortune and face hardship together.” You had no desire to enter these troubled waters, yet could not afford to offend them, so he had always put them off with agreeable words. That had been possible before. Now that the time had come for real swords and spears, agreeable words were no longer enough. “I shall speak to him,” the Seventh Lady said, swearing under her breath in her usual coarse fashion. “Damn it! There is such a thing as forced sex, but not forced gambling. Rebellion is not an evening with singing girls. How can they drag someone along against his will?” “There you go again!” Mrs You was both angry and anxious. “Please, my dear lady! If you mean to quarrel with him, you had better not go.” “Oh, Fifth Sister-in-Law, you still take me for such a fool! I am only grumbling here. Once we meet, he is a guest. Why should I offend him without cause?” She urged Mrs You towards the door. “Go and attend to him first. Be especially courteous; do not leave him feeling neglected.” “There is no need to worry. I have had breakfast served, and he is drinking some wine. He travelled all night to get here.” “Then, when he has finished, ask him to meet me in Brother Five’s room.”

You had a private meeting room in what appeared to be an isolated courtyard, cut off on every side, though in fact a tunnel connected it with the outside. Fearing that word might leak out, the Seventh Lady deliberately chose this place for their conversation. The visitor was a clansman of Zhou Lichun’s, sixth in his generation, and she knew him too. But for business of this kind, personal acquaintance was not enough; credentials were required. As soon as they met, she asked, “Brother Zhou Liu, what is it you wish to discuss with Brother Five?” Zhou Liu hesitated. “Seventh Lady, Lichun has a few confidential words...” “A moment, Brother Zhou Liu.” She stopped him. “If they are Brother Zhou Lichun’s confidential words, you know the rule?” “Ah, I had forgotten.” With an apologetic smile, he reached into his waistband and produced a piece of Han-dynasty jade. This was his credential. Planning rebellion was a secret matter that could cost a man his head, so Zhou Lichun could not commit their dealings to writing. Yet a messenger’s unsupported word was no proof. He and You had therefore agreed that this jade would authenticate any message. Without it, lips must remain sealed. The Seventh Lady knew the arrangement and had asked for it at once. Having verified the piece, she returned it. “Brother Zhou Liu, you know how things are managed here. You may speak to me just as you would to my brother.”

“Yes, yes. We know that the Seventh Lady has the mettle of a man and that your brother consults you in every important affair.” Zhou Liu glanced uneasily outside, then lowered his voice almost to a whisper. “You have heard the news from Shanghai, I suppose?” “Only just. I do not yet know the details.” “Shanghai has succeeded. Everything has gone smoothly for Brother Liu, and it will go more smoothly still. Most of the Green Standard soldiers at Suzhou are from Huzhou, his own home district. They have already agreed to rise. Lichun intends to act within the next two or three days.” Zhou paused, then continued with some difficulty. “He discussed it with Brother Five You before, and You promised to help when the time came. That is what I have come about.” “I know you discussed the matter,” she answered without haste. “But I never heard Brother Five promise that he would certainly help.” There was no obvious way to continue after that. Zhou sat dumbfounded, his face full of disappointment.

“Brother Zhou Liu, no one values loyalty more than my brother. For a friend, he would climb a mountain of blades or plunge into boiling oil. Would he not?” “Indeed!” Zhou nodded repeatedly. “That is why Lichun asked for his help. We should share good fortune and face hardship together.” “To tell you the truth, my brother is facing hardship himself at this very moment.” She seized the opening. “A year or two ago, if he had made excuses, he would have been a contemptible bastard. Now he truly has the will but not the means. Why? It all comes back to that damned sea transport, dreamed up by some corrupt official!” “Sea transport? You mean sending the grain tax by sea?” “Exactly. It fattens the purse of the Sand-Boat Guild. Their vessels used to sail north towards Manchuria carrying nothing but stone ballast. Now they carry tax rice instead and earn freight money for what was once an empty voyage. If they reach Tianjin without mishap, there are recommendations for official rewards as well. Even the guild leaders are becoming officials. Is that not enough to make one furious?” She swallowed and continued. “The sand-boat men are enjoying their cursed good fortune, while our Grain Transport Brotherhood is losing its livelihood. You know Songjiang is one of the impoverished branches. Keeping this household of men going has been like eating bitter coptis root instead of rice for my brother—nothing but hardship. The Double Ninth Festival will soon be here, and the northwest winds will rise, yet the brothers’ lined coats are still in the pawnshops. He has to find some means of helping them. At present he has gone to Shanghai with an outsider to trade in silk, hoping to scrape together something to fill the gaps. Think of his standing in our world, Brother Zhou Liu! Would he attend on an outsider unless poverty left him no choice? He is like a clay Buddha crossing a river, unable even to save himself. How can he help Brother Zhou Lichun?”

Zhou was left speechless. After a long pause, he managed to ask, “Then why did he promise to help when the time came?” “That is the sort of man he is. Ask him now, and he will still promise. But in my opinion, the more he helped, the more trouble he would cause.” “Oh?” Zhou was astonished. “Why should that be?” “Because men have to eat.” Her answer was crisp. “Why was the grain tax diverted to the sea? They say the canal is too shallow and the grain boats sometimes cannot pass. One can find a remedy for that. But if disorder makes the route impassable, that is a complete dead end. The brothers already shake their heads at the Longhairs. Ask them to follow Brother Zhou Lichun now, and they may say nothing openly while thinking something quite different. If they did something disloyal, my brother could certainly not hold them down. Would his help not make matters worse?” Zhou shuddered. If the Songjiang brotherhood joined the rising and, once it had foreign guns in its hands, turned them on its supposed allies, that would be no laughing matter.

On reflection, however, the argument did not seem right to him. Zhou had seen the brotherhood’s canonical text, the Tongcao, whose title was colloquially written with the similar-sounding character for “grass” in place of “grain transport.” It recorded how Patriarch Lu sent the three patriarchs Weng, Qian, and Pan down from the mountain to spread the Way—the Way of overthrowing the Qing and restoring the Ming. Of the two verses spoken by Lu, the first contained the line “The later generation shall recover the world of those before,” referring to the recovery of the Ming realm. In the second, “Sun and moon shine high upon the jade vessel,” the written characters for sun and moon combined to make Ming, while the word for vessel, hu, sounded like the word for the northern peoples and referred to the Qing. That too implied overthrowing the Qing and restoring the Ming. How, then, could the brotherhood turn against a rising directed against the Qing? He voiced his thoughts, only to receive a scornful reply. “Brother Zhou Liu, who knows how long ago those doctrines were handed down? Even an emperor cannot send hungry soldiers to fight. With no food to eat, is it not ridiculous to dream of the Ming realm now?” There was no point in pursuing the matter. His journey had been wasted. After thinking for a moment, Zhou said, “Then let us regard everything I have said today as unsaid, Seventh Lady. You may treat it as something you never heard.” She understood. “Set your mind at rest. I would never be such a bungler. If a single word of what you have told me escapes, come and call my brother and me to account.” She continued with great sincerity. “I truly regret that you have made this journey for nothing. But the situation is plain: we cannot do what we would wish. Please tell Brother Zhou Lichun that we are sorry to fail him this time. If there is anything else in which we can be useful, he has only to ask. We too may need his protection one day. Send a spring breeze, and summer rain will follow. As long as it is within our power, helping a friend is helping ourselves.”

Zhou nodded inwardly. People said that the Seventh Lady conducted affairs as capably as any man, and her reputation was justified. Her last words also carried an appeal. Even if the business had failed, the friendship should be maintained; he might as well show her the consideration she sought. “Since that is what you say, Seventh Lady, you may be entirely reassured. From Jiading one comes to Qingpu, and from Qingpu to Songjiang. If we reach your district in a few days, with the Old Master here, we would never presume to cause a disturbance.” “Brother Zhou Liu, those words are worth something. I thank you on behalf of the people of Songjiang.” She clasped her hands and bowed in the manner of a man. Harmony had at least been preserved. After seeing Zhou out through the back door, she could not help feeling pleased with herself and returned to the rear quarters smiling. Mrs You came to meet her. “What was said?” “It is all settled.” She kept her promise to Zhou. “There is no need to go into the details. In a word, I have swept away every one of Brother Five’s difficulties.”

“We are fortunate to have you!” Mrs You was deeply relieved. “We should thank Mr Hu too. Without him, your brother would never have gone to Shanghai. You have handled this better than he could have done himself.” “That is true.” After considering, the Seventh Lady said, “Fifth Sister-in-Law, I must go to Shanghai today.” “You ought to. I only fear the journey may be difficult.” “What is there to fear?” She was unconcerned. “They are making trouble on land. We shall go by boat and never encounter them. Even if we did, would I be afraid?” “Then go as soon as you can. Tell Brother Five to stay out of the way there for a while, so that those troublemakers do not come looking for him again.” “I understand. I shall pack. Please have a boat made ready at once.”

She returned to her bedroom and hurriedly gathered the clothes she would need. While she was busy, A’zhu slipped in with a request. “Seventh Sister, I do not care what you say—you must take me with you.” “Eh?” The Seventh Lady was surprised. “I am not going for an outing.” “Neither am I. I want to see Father. Otherwise I cannot feel easy.” “That is understandable, but the journey is difficult. The roads are unsettled.” She spoke gravely. “Think of it: what rebel has any respect for law or restraint? Meeting them would be no joke.” “I am not afraid!” A’zhu declared recklessly. “At worst, I have only one life to lose.” “They may spare your life and assault you instead.” That frightened her. After a pause, she asked, “What about you?” “I shall be all right. I can face them and settle things directly. Besides, I have trained in martial arts. Three or five fellows like A’long would be no match for me.” Taking a green sugar cane from the corner, she struck it with the edge of her right palm. She seemed to use scarcely any force, yet the cane broke in two. Her explanation and demonstration had exactly the opposite effect from the one intended. A’zhu already trusted her. Now, seeing this display of skill, she felt safer still. “With a woman bodyguard to protect me, what have I to fear?” she said lightly. “I am definitely coming. I shall pack too.”

“A moment, a moment.” The Seventh Lady caught her and thought it over again. Finally, with a helpless nod, she yielded. “If you insist, I shall take you. But frankly, bringing someone as young and pretty as you places a heavy responsibility on me. You must do as I say, or else...” “I will, I will!” A’zhu interrupted eagerly. “Whatever you say, I shall do.” “Then you have travelled enough to know that women have their own crude precautions. Have you any undertrousers of coarse cloth?” A’zhu had heard of this precaution and was quite willing to try it, but she had no coarse-cloth pair. “Then wear several pairs.” She obeyed, putting on three pairs of undertrousers and two close-fitting little waistcoats. Back in the Seventh Lady’s room, with the door firmly shut, they sewed the waistbands, trouser cuffs, and waistcoat fronts securely shut. The intention was to make it difficult for an attacker to get through the clothing.

After lunch, just as they were preparing to board, an unexpected visitor arrived: Chen Shilong. He was covered in mud and looked thoroughly bedraggled, but his spirits were high. His face showed the satisfaction of a man who had come through danger and reached his destination safely. The household immediately gathered around him, all eager for news of Shanghai. The Seventh Lady and A’zhu postponed their departure; they would hear what he had to say before deciding what to do. “How did you get here?” Mrs You asked urgently. “Our people are all well, I hope?” “All well, all well!” Chen answered loudly. “They are staying in the foreign settlement. Perfectly safe.” This reassured everyone. “And the county town?” she asked. “The town has fallen.” Chen had a fairly complete understanding of events and began at the beginning. “There had long been rumours that the Small Swords Society intended to rise. The trouble lay with Circuit Intendant Wu...”

He meant Wu Jianzhang, the military intendant of the Suzhou-Songjiang-Taicang circuit. Wu and Liu Lichuan came from the same province and were old acquaintances. Moreover, many of the Shanghai county militia were men from Guangdong and Fujian. Wu therefore paid little attention to rumours that the Small Swords Society would use the militia to launch a rising. In his view, such a rising would be an act against him personally. Given their friendship, Liu would never do anything so disloyal. Yet Liu had already made contact with Luo Dagang, a chief minister of the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom, and with the British consul, Wen Nazhi. He decided to rise on the day of the Confucian sacrifice and attack the county yamen first. Shanghai’s magistrate was Yuan Zude, a grandson of Yuan Zicai. Having purchased office as deputy magistrate of Baoshan, he had risen to the Shanghai magistracy. Early that morning he dressed formally and prepared to take his sedan to the Confucian temple for the sacrifice. He had just emerged from the main hall when a band of men with red cloths wound around their heads burst in. Their leader, Little Jin, had once been arrested and punished by Yuan as a hooligan. At the sight of his old enemy, his anger blazed; a bright blade was thrust towards Yuan’s chest. Yuan was a man of courage. He cursed them bitterly and died without yielding. On hearing the news, Wu fled to the British consulate and escaped with his life. The circuit offices, county offices, and customs house were attacked in succession. The Small Swords men established themselves in a newly built mansion belonging to Yu Fushan, a magnate of the Sand-Boat Guild, at Qiaojiabin near the Little South Gate. The city was in great disorder, but the Red Turbans dared not set foot in the foreign settlement. Refugees poured there for safety, making its ten-li extent busier than ever.

“What about the government troops?” the Seventh Lady asked. “Did they not even fight?” “There were very few of them. They did not dare fight at all. Their commander, a garrison officer surnamed Li, hanged himself.” “Duck dung!” she said contemptuously. “If he had the nerve to hang himself, why not fight?” “Let us leave these other people’s affairs alone,” Mrs You said. “How did you get here?” “I came specially with a message—a spoken message.” Chen looked around. “May we go inside to discuss it?” The information was plainly confidential. Once they had moved into the inner hall, he told Mrs You that You Laowu had particularly instructed them to deal courteously with anyone who came from Jiading and, above all, not to give offence. “So that is the message!” the Seventh Lady said. “Why did they send you?” It was a reasonable question. You had plenty of men of his own; a message of this kind should have been entrusted to one of them. Why trouble Chen, who was a guest?

“There is a reason,” Chen explained. “Mr Hu asked me to take Miss Zhu back to Huzhou. As I was coming this way, I was to bring the message too.” “But...” The Seventh Lady was greatly surprised. “Why is that?” “Mr Hu says that with war and disorder everywhere, she would be better off at home. Mr Zhang says the same.” “We must ask her.” Then she suddenly added, “Here is what we shall do. We have already arranged to go to Shanghai together, and the boat is ready. Come with us. Whatever needs discussing can be discussed when we get there.”

“Very well. When do we leave?” Chen looked down at himself. “I am covered in mud. I must have a bath first.” While he was at the bathhouse, the Seventh Lady sought out A’zhu, who had withdrawn to let them discuss the confidential message. She explained the real purpose of Chen’s journey and her own decision. A’zhu naturally agreed, though she wondered why Hu, who must be badly in need of helpers just now, was willing to send Chen on a special journey to escort her home. The Seventh Lady was shrewd enough to understand at once that Hu was making an opportunity for Chen. A’zhu was uncertain of her future, Chen was deeply attached to her, and some affection had already grown between them. A long journey together might allow their feelings to develop further. Yet the Seventh Lady believed she understood the two better than Hu did and was confident that she could help bring about a suitable match. She therefore took it upon herself to change his arrangements.

Their boat entered the Wusong River and, favoured by both wind and current, reached Shanghai after a single night. They dared not moor at the Little East Gate this time. Landing at Yangjingbang, they took sedan chairs directly to the Yuji Silk Warehouse. The place was in chaos. Even the corridors were covered with makeshift bedding. Refugees from the county town and the Pudong area, all connected with the household by some tie of kinship or acquaintance, had half begged and half forced their way into lodging there. It was the Seventh Lady’s first visit too. At the sight of the crowd, she cried, “How can anyone live here? Where are Brother Five and the others?” “Do not worry. There is room.” Chen led the two women straight to the back, where another black-painted, stone-framed gate stood slightly ajar. Beyond it was quite a different world: a two-storey building three bays wide, stacked with bales of silk. “A’zhu!” She looked up and saw her father calling from an open upstairs window. “The silk is downstairs; the people sleep above,” Chen explained. “Let us go up first.” Zhang came down to meet them and led them upstairs. After the upheaval they had endured, father and daughter felt almost as though they were meeting in another lifetime. When they were seated, the Seventh Lady asked, “Where are they?” She meant You and Hu. “Some foreigners have invited them to a Western meal to discuss business. They should be back soon.” Zhang turned to his daughter. “Xueyan and I agreed that Shilong should take you to Huzhou. Why have you come to Shanghai instead?” “It was my idea,” the Seventh Lady answered quickly. “It was easy enough to arrange. But let us say no more for now. Mr Zhang, forgive me, but would you sit downstairs for a little while? We need to use the room.”

This was exactly what A’zhu wanted. Since taking that “crude precaution,” she had found the restrictions most inconvenient and had scarcely dared drink any tea. She was eager to undo the fastenings and be comfortable again. “Father, please go down for a little while,” she urged. “Quickly!” Zhang was puzzled, but saw no need to inquire into women’s matters. He took his tobacco pipe and left. Chen naturally had to go too. Pointing to either side, he said, “Both rooms are open. Use whichever you please.” “A’long!” The Seventh Lady called him back. For once, even this woman who scarcely knew the meaning of embarrassment looked a little awkward. She smiled sheepishly. “May I trouble you with something? I do not know whether they have a maid here, or where the main kitchen is. Could you bring us a bucket of hot water?” “Of course.” Chen understood quickly. “There is a newly bought washbasin in Mr Hu’s room. You may use it.” He hurried downstairs. “Look,” the Seventh Lady whispered teasingly to A’zhu. “A’long has gone to fetch your washing water.” A’zhu had no attention to spare for jokes and hurried into the room. The Seventh Lady followed. Both worked quickly: they closed the doors and windows, helped each other in the darkness, and undid the protective stitching. Before long they heard Chen on the stairs, bringing a kettle of hot water and a bucket of cold. Having explained which was which, he prepared to go down again.

“A’long, wait!” the Seventh Lady called. “What are we to do in the dark? Bring us a light.” The room happened to be the one he shared with Old Zhang. “There is a foreign candle on my table and a packet of red-headed matches under my pillow,” he answered. “Which bed is yours?” “The one against the wall. The matches will light if you strike them anywhere. Be careful not to burn your hand.” “I understand. Do not go yet; there is something else I want you to do.”

The Seventh Lady found the matches and struck one on the floor. A’zhu immediately blew it out, concerned that the gaps in the partition might compromise their privacy. The Seventh Lady called to Chen to ask what he was doing outside. “I am sitting here, waiting to see what else you need.” She teased him about lingering and told him to respect their privacy. He smiled without answering. A’zhu quietly reproached her for drawing attention to the matter and asked her not to light the candle. Chen heard this and decided that proper conduct mattered more than anything else. “If there is nothing more, I shall go downstairs,” he called. The Seventh Lady agreed that he should withdraw. “Thank you. Please watch the stairs and make sure nobody comes up unexpectedly.” With him guarding the staircase, they could feel secure. She fetched the washbasin from Hu’s room and brought in the water. After washing, they took out their grooming things, arranged their hair, put on their cosmetics, and changed into clean clothes. Only then did they open the door.

By coincidence, the proprietor’s wife had just heard that women guests had arrived and came over with a maid for heavy work and a younger maid. The Seventh Lady knew her and greeted her as Mrs Chen, then introduced A’zhu. While the older maid put their upstairs room in order, host and guests settled down to exchange courtesies and discuss the journey. Mrs Chen invited them to stay at her own house. The Seventh Lady feared the restrictions of being a guest and did not wish to go. When she consulted A’zhu, the girl agreed and offered the excuse that, having seen her father, she would soon return to Huzhou, so there was no need to make further arrangements. The Seventh Lady added her own polite refusals, and Mrs Chen had to accept them. After sitting a while, she invited them to dinner. The Seventh Lady agreed to come once she had seen her brother and finished their business. When Mrs Chen left, Chen Shilong arranged the beds for them. He and Old Zhang moved downstairs and made sleeping places beside the bales of silk. Their former room contained a large bed and a small one. The Seventh Lady took the large bed; A’zhu had the small one, which had previously been Chen’s.

The arrangements had barely been completed when Hu and You returned to the depot. A different time and place produced different feelings: Hu was composed as ever, and A’zhu too seemed at ease. The Seventh Lady briefly explained why she had decided to come to Shanghai, then signalled to her brother that she wanted a private conversation. You now shared confidential matters with Hu and drew him along to hear her report. “The man from Jiading came yesterday morning...” She gave a detailed account. “That was a good way to handle it,” You said, relieved. Listening quietly, Hu had not expected the Seventh Lady to be so capable and regarded her with new respect. She noticed his look and was pleased. “Young Uncle,” she asked with a smile, “do you think I said anything wrong?” “Certainly not!” Hu turned to You. “That removes one worry. Now we can give proper thought to our affairs in Shanghai.” Before replying to him, You spoke quietly to his sister. “A’qi, I cannot return just yet, and I am anxious about things at home. The route should still be passable for a day or two. You had better go back at once.”

She nodded, then asked about their affairs in Shanghai. “How is business?” You had no ready answer. He merely sighed faintly, showing that matters were not going smoothly. Hu, however, remained optimistic. “Very good. We are negotiating and should have a result soon.” In fact, agreement would not be easy. Hu was holding firm and refusing to sell, while the foreign firms were waiting to see what would happen after the Small Swords uprising. Tea and silk, the two largest items in the export trade, still had quoted prices but scarcely any transactions; the whole market was in confusion. You knew little about commerce and, with the political situation so unsettled, naturally felt pessimistic. That was why he had sighed instead of answering. “A’qi,” he repeated, “go back tomorrow.”

“I know!” the Seventh Lady replied with displeasure. “I shall go. But I brought our sister Zhang to Shanghai, and I must make some arrangement for her.” “Leave her in her father’s care.” That was reasonable, but the Seventh Lady was intent on tying the red thread of marriage and wanted a settlement at once. She could hardly say so openly and fell silent. Hu understood her enthusiasm. “Seventh Sister, there will certainly be a proper arrangement. It is no use hurrying. I mean to send her back to Huzhou with Shilong. That, too, would count as making provision for her.” “Mm, mm.” She committed herself to neither agreement nor disagreement. Then she said, “The proprietor’s wife has invited us all to dinner tonight. It is time to go.” “We cannot,” You replied, shaking his head. “We have arranged to meet an important man this evening. Go without us.” They had scarcely met before they parted again. Without even time to warm their seats, You and Hu hurried away to keep an appointment at a courtesan house.
